title: Alliance Role
description: Find the alliance job you are built for: 1ic, 2ic, MA, FA, IA, EI, TA, or JA.

1ic.label: 1ic
1ic.summary: You fit the top executive role: final calls, direction, standards, and the burden of owning outcomes.

2ic.label: 2ic
2ic.summary: You fit the deputy/operator role: translating vision into action, coordinating departments, and keeping leadership aligned.

MA.label: MA
MA.summary: You fit Military Affairs: wars, counters, readiness, target selection, and tactical execution.

FA.label: FA
FA.summary: You fit Foreign Affairs: diplomacy, treaties, reputation, coalition awareness, and careful negotiation.

IA.label: IA
IA.summary: You fit Internal Affairs: recruitment, onboarding, retention, member care, and alliance culture.

EI.label: EI
EI.summary: You fit Economic/Internal finance work: banks, grants, taxes, city growth, audits, and resource planning.

TA.label: TA
TA.summary: You fit Technical Affairs: tools, automation, sheets, bots, data hygiene, and systems that make everyone faster.

JA.label: JA
JA.summary: You fit Junior Affairs: learning fast, helping where needed, handling starter tasks, and growing into a department.

questions.prompt: A new member asks what they should do first after joining. What do you naturally handle?

answers.text: Give them the starter checklist, answer questions, and make sure they feel welcomed.
Check their build, income path, and whether they qualify for grants.
Point them to war policy, MMR expectations, and defensive readiness basics.
Make sure they have the right roles, channels, and tool access.

questions.prompt: Two government members disagree in public chat. Your first instinct is to:

answers.text: Move the discussion private, settle the decision, and set expectations for conduct.
Clarify each person's tasking and turn the disagreement into an action list.
Check whether member morale or confusion caused the argument.
Keep notes, ask what support is needed, and learn from how senior staff resolve it.

questions.prompt: True or false: During a war, organized target selection and counter timing matter more than individual bravado.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: A treaty partner sends a tense DM about a raid from one of your members. What do you focus on?

answers.text: De-escalate, get facts, protect the relationship, and avoid overpromising.
Confirm whether the raid violates policy and coordinate any military response.
Review whether the member was trained clearly on raid rules.
Ask a senior FA member what information they need and help collect it.

questions.prompt: Which task sounds most satisfying after a long day?

answers.text: Cleaning up a spreadsheet so grant approvals are faster and less error-prone.
Reviewing applicants and turning inactive members into active ones.
Reading global politics and identifying which blocs are drifting closer.
Running war rooms and watching a clean counter chain land.

questions.prompt: True or false: A good alliance bank needs clear records, permissions, and audit trails.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: Leadership needs one person to turn a vague plan into assignments. You would rather:

answers.text: Define the objective, choose owners, set deadlines, and check progress.
Decide whether the plan fits the alliance's long-term direction.
Build a tracker so everyone can see task status.
Take a small assignment and execute it reliably.

questions.prompt: A member is underbuilt for their city count. Your response is:

answers.text: Calculate the most efficient correction path and explain the grant/tax impact.
Check if their build harms war readiness and set minimum military expectations.
Walk them through the fix patiently and keep them engaged.
Ask for the approved build guide and help compare it to their nation.

questions.prompt: True or false: Private channels, logs, and permissions are part of alliance security, not just convenience.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: You are asked to represent the alliance in a coalition server. What matters most?

answers.text: Speak carefully, understand incentives, and keep private positions private.
Track military commitments, counters, and target lists accurately.
Know what the alliance leader will and will not approve.
Observe, take notes, and avoid speaking beyond your assignment.

questions.prompt: A department has gone quiet for a week. What do you do?

answers.text: Check blockers, reassign work if needed, and get the department moving again.
Decide whether the department lead still fits the role.
Find small tasks newer helpers can complete to restart momentum.
Automate reminders or reporting so silence is spotted sooner.

questions.prompt: Pick the report you would most want to write.

answers.text: War readiness, counters performed, beige discipline, and rebuild needs.
Recruitment funnel, retention risks, onboarding completion, and activity.
Bank flows, city grants, resource exposure, and growth efficiency.
Foreign contacts, treaty status, bloc movement, and reputation risks.

questions.prompt: True or false: A 1ic should be willing to make unpopular calls when the alliance needs clarity.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: A bot command breaks right before a major operation. Your role is:

answers.text: Debug the command, patch it, and communicate the workaround.
Switch the operation to manual tracking and keep people moving.
Make sure members know what to do without panic.
Run the manual task assigned to you and report problems quickly.

questions.prompt: Which alliance problem bothers you the most?

answers.text: No clear direction from the top.
Good plans dying because nobody coordinates execution.
Members feeling ignored or confused.
Manual data entry wasting hours every week.

questions.prompt: A rebuild after war is messy. Where do you jump in?

answers.text: Prioritize who needs aid, estimate costs, and keep bank exposure under control.
Review military losses and rebuild order for future readiness.
Message damaged members and keep them from checking out.
Gather damage reports into one clean tracker.

questions.prompt: True or false: Diplomacy is partly about knowing when not to speak.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: You are given access to sensitive alliance data. What is your default posture?

answers.text: Least privilege, logs, backups, and no casual sharing.
Only use it for approved financial decisions and keep records clean.
Protect operational data so enemies cannot exploit timing or targets.
Ask what you are allowed to see and who to report to.

questions.prompt: Which phrase sounds most like you in government chat?

answers.text: What decision are we making, and who owns it?
What does this do to our long-term position?
What does the data say?
What can I take off someone's plate?

questions.prompt: An applicant has strong stats but a questionable history. What lens do you use first?

answers.text: Security, culture fit, and whether they are worth the risk.
Past alliance relationships and whether accepting them causes FA fallout.
Activity, attitude, and whether onboarding can correct the concerns.
Ask senior staff what checks they want completed.

questions.prompt: True or false: Junior government work is valuable when it is consistent, documented, and easy for senior staff to verify.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: You have one free evening to improve the alliance. You choose:

answers.text: Rewrite outdated onboarding and follow up with quiet members.
Build a tool that removes repeated manual checks.
Audit grants, taxes, and missed growth opportunities.
Review recent wars and improve counter doctrine.

questions.prompt: A rival alliance offers a tempting deal with hidden risks. Your best contribution is:

answers.text: Read the room politically and identify what each side really wants.
Decide if the deal fits the alliance identity and risk tolerance.
Model the military commitments it could create.
Organize notes, timelines, and follow-up questions.

questions.prompt: Which metric do you watch first during peacetime?

answers.text: Member activity, retention, and onboarding completion.
Net revenue, grant velocity, and bank liquidity.
Readiness, MMR compliance, and target range health.
Tool uptime, data freshness, and permission errors.

questions.prompt: True or false: If nobody owns a deadline, a 2ic-type operator should force clarity.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: A member posts inaccurate war advice. How do you handle it?

answers.text: Correct it clearly with the right mechanic and explain why it matters.
Move the correction into a guide so the mistake does not repeat.
Ask a senior MA person to verify before you amplify the correction.
Check if a tool or guide is out of date and caused the confusion.

questions.prompt: What kind of pressure are you most comfortable carrying?

answers.text: Being accountable for the final alliance-wide decision.
Making sure every department actually executes.
Handling hostile conversations without escalating them.
Owning a smaller task and proving you can be trusted with more.

questions.prompt: Which alliance channel would you most likely keep pinned and organized?

answers.text: War room: targets, counters, beige rules, and rebuild instructions.
Embassy: contact notes, treaty terms, and active diplomatic threads.
Internal guides: onboarding, grants, rules, and member help.
Tech ops: bot status, feature requests, data issues, and permissions.

questions.prompt: True or false: Economic advice should account for alliance policy, not just personal profit.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: A major announcement needs to go out. What do you contribute?

answers.text: Set the actual policy and own the final wording.
Make sure every department knows what changes after the announcement.
Write it in a way members understand and respond to.
Prepare links, forms, embeds, or automation attached to it.

questions.prompt: Which mistake do you most want to prevent?

answers.text: Entering a war without readiness or counter coordination.
Signing or rejecting a treaty without understanding political consequences.
Letting members go inactive because nobody followed up.
Losing money because records, grants, or permissions are sloppy.

questions.prompt: When you are new to a government team, your best path is:

answers.text: Learn the systems, do assigned tasks reliably, and ask for feedback.
Find a neglected process and quietly improve it.
Help onboard other newer members once you understand the basics.
Study alliance doctrine until you can explain the why behind orders.
